issues.legal_issue: A final quasi-judicial permission to institute an eviction suit cannot be challenged collaterally in that suit on the ground that the deciding authority made an error within its jurisdiction.
material_facts: The landlord obtained permission to sue for eviction from the Rent Control and Eviction Officer, who found the landlord’s need bona fide and genuine.
The Additional Commissioner confirmed the permission, and the tenant did not seek review by the State Government.
In the eviction suits, the tenant argued that the permission was invalid because the officer had not considered the tenant’s need.
The authority had jurisdiction to decide the permission application; the alleged failure was, at most, an error in reaching its decision.
issues.conclusion: The permission could not be challenged in the eviction suits. Any error in the decision had to be pursued through the statutory review procedure or by seeking an appropriate writ, not through a collateral challenge in the suits.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 3(2), 3(3) and 3(4) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, the permission proceedings before the District Magistrate or delegated officer and the Commissioner are quasi-judicial, and the Commissioner’s decision is final subject to an order under section 7-F. Section 16 does not exclude the High Court’s jurisdiction under Article 226, but the decision, subject to such High Court interference, cannot be challenged in a collateral proceeding. An error made by an authority having jurisdiction is not, merely because it is erroneous, a decision without jurisdiction or contrary to natural justice; correction must be sought through the statutory route or an appropriate writ. Shri Bhagwan v. Ram Chand was distinguished, and Asa Singh v. B. D. Sanwal was held inapplicable because it arose in a writ proceeding, not an eviction suit challenging permission collaterally.

rule.if: eviction_suit and quasi_judicial_permission and competent_decision_maker and final_review_order and not statutory_review_invoked

predicates.eviction_suit: The proceeding in which the permission is challenged is a suit brought to obtain eviction.
predicates.quasi_judicial_permission: An authority made a quasi-judicial decision granting permission to institute the eviction suit.
predicates.competent_decision_maker: The authority had jurisdiction to hear and decide the permission application.
predicates.final_review_order: The decision became final under the applicable review structure, subject to any available supervisory writ jurisdiction.
predicates.statutory_review_invoked: The affected person sought review through the statutory procedure.

issues.definition: When a competent authority’s quasi-judicial permission becomes final and statutory review has not been invoked, the permission cannot be challenged collaterally in an eviction suit.
